newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico mark Eurobond may be used for Brady buyback.
newsitem.headline: Mexico mark Eurobond may be used for Brady buyback.

text.p: For the third time in less than a month, Mexico plans to tap capital markets, aiming to beat any possible mid-year market turmoil, diversify its debt portfolio -- and perhaps replace some outstanding Brady bonds, analysts said on Monday.
In Frankfurt on Monday, Guillermo Ortiz told reporters that Mexico plans to issue a 12-year mark-denominated Eurobond for one billion marks ($609.3 million).

The bond is seen yielding 260 to 280 basis points over the new German 10-year six-percent government issue. Deutsche Morgan Grenfell and Dresdner Kleinwort Benson are joint lead managers for the issue.
With key mid-term elections planned this July, Mexico has rushed to embrace receptive investors before what could be a period of intense interest rate volatility.

Mexico tapped the German market last year when it placed an eight-year one billion mark ($675 million) structured issue that was later bumped up by another 500 million marks. The issue paid 304 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
The federal government only has $1.4 billion in maturing market debt this year, but officials have said they are also considering buying back outstanding Aztec Brady bonds.

"Payments for this year are almost covered, but it would be beneficial to keep substituting cheaper debt with better terms for more expensive debt, which is one of our aims," Ortiz told reporters in Paris last week.
The Aztec bonds could be called at the end of March or purchased in the market. The spread on the Aztec bonds is much higher than recently placed market debt.

U.S. Treasury zero-coupon bond collateral represents almost half the value of the Aztecs, so replacing $2.0 billion of the outstanding Aztecs could be done with a new issuance of only half the size, analysts have said.
With the new mark issue aimed at financing "short-term" Mexican liabilities, according to Ortiz, analysts said this could mean another Brady buyback.
"I get the sense that this could be what they are alluding to," said Santander Investment debt analyst Julian Eisner.
Mexico has been busy in markets recently.

Last week, the federal government also placed a 10-year 500 billion Italian lira bond, worth about $310 million, aimed at refinancing maturing debt in 1997 and at extending Mexico's base of investors.
Mexico placed a $1.0 billion 10-year fixed rate global issue in early January, at 337.5 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
It used the funds as part of what it used to pay back the United States Treasury and the International Monetary Fund.

Government officials have clearly said they hoped to broaden the currency base of Mexico's external debt, particularly in Europe, after having focused heavily on Japanese yen, marks and U.S. dollar issues since making a return to markets after the peso crash.
Last week Ortiz started a visit to France; Davos, Switzerland; and to Germany, aimed at tightening economic and financial ties and promoting investment opportunities in Mexico.
Mexico is also studying placing an issue denominated in French francs, Ortiz said in Paris last week.
Analysts said the spread on the latest mark offering from Mexico is seen as tight, as there are no other issues coming due at the same time.
